subject: safe pointer alloc and free (command refactor)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: safe pointer alloc and free (command refactor)
parts:
Looking at src/stan/gm/command.hpp, there are unsafe pointer allocations.
To be safe, you really need to put the allocation in a
try block and then a free in a catch block, as so:

try {
malloc/new
...
} catch (exception& e) {
free/delete
}
free / delete

The first case deletes if there's an exception and the
second if there's not. This is all encapsulated in Java's
finally block, but we don't get that sugar in C++. You
can define a cleanup function and reuse it if it's more
than a single statement.

And, nothing in the ... after the malloc should return
and potentially get by the free/delete ops.

If you don't follow this pattern, you have to be really
really careful to free everything that gets allocated
some other way, which can be very error prone because
now you're tracing through spaghetti rather than simple
block scopes.

I would *very strongly* prefer we don't use malloc or new
if we can avoid it. On that note, let's see how that's done.

Here's what's in the gm/command.hpp now:


int sampler_select = engine_index + 10 * metric_index + 100 * static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged);

switch (sampler_select) {

case 0: {
typedef stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc<Model, rng_t> sampler;
sampler_ptr = new sampler(model, base_rng);
if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(sampler_ptr, algo)) return 0;
break;
}

case 1: {
typedef stan::mcmc::unit_e_nuts<Model, rng_t> sampler;
sampler_ptr = new sampler(model, base_rng);
if (!init_nuts<sampler>(sampler_ptr, algo)) return 0;
break;
}

}
...do something with sampler_ptr...

if (sampler_ptr) delete sampler_ptr;


Note that if you hit one of the return statements in the case
statement, you bypass the delete of the sampler_ptr and leak memory.
Probably not a big deal here in terms of leakage because you are just
going to exit the command, but it'll light up all the debugging tools
as an error, and it'd be better not to have more false positives than
we already get in agrad.

Here's how I'd rewrite this code to avoid using pointers:

switch (sampler_select) {
case 0: {
typedef stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc<Model, rng_t> sampler;
sampler s(model, base_rng);
if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(s, algo))
return 0;
return sample(s, ...);
}
}

where the ... are the other variables needed to run the sampler.
The sample() function is then templated on the sampler type:

template <class S>
int sample(S& s, ...) {
... do something with s ...
}

The type S gets inferred from the argument, which is now
properly typed rather than being a made-poor-decisions pointer (I think
that's the PC way to describe the opposite of a smart pointer --- we
wouldn't want to say "dumb" or "stupid" lest the code get offended).

In fact, I'd be tempted to have the sampler class have a flag indicating
whether to call that init_static thing so that it's part of sample, as in:

switch (sampler_select) {
case 0:
return sample(stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc(model,base_rng),
...);


template <class S>
int sample(S& s, ...) {
if (s.requires_init_static())
if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(s, algo))
return 0;
... do something with s...
return 0; // normal return
}

You could probably just have something like s::requires_init_static
as a static boolean class variable so you don't even need a method.

Also, should that return from the conditional on init_static_hmc
failing be 0 or something indicating a failure to initialize?

Now everything's safe from leaking memory. And there's less
duplicated code.

I'd be happy to go through and do the refactoring. I
opened an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/390

and assigned it to myself.

- Bob

P.S. I'd also much rather see the numerically obfuscated switch replaced
with an if-then structure. But I can see how reasonable people would
differ on this preference.

P.P.S. Why static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged); Isn't adapt_engaged already
boolean? You just want to be explicit?

P.P.P.S. It's good style to declare variables close to where you define them.
The sampler_ptr was defined way before the case statement to set it
and not used in between. But that'll be moot once we get rid of
the pointers.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] safe pointer alloc and free (command refactor)
parts:
> In fact, I'd be tempted to have the sampler class have a flag indicating
> whether to call that init_static thing so that it's part of sample, as in:
>
> switch (sampler_select) {
> case 0:
> return sample(stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc(model,base_rng),
> ...);
>
>
> template <class S>
> int sample(S& s, ...) {
> if (s.requires_init_static())
> if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(s, algo))
> return 0;
> ... do something with s...
> return 0; // normal return
> }
>
> You could probably just have something like s::requires_init_static
> as a static boolean class variable so you don't even need a method.

But then we'd have to have each sampler implementation be aware
of all other implementations through the possible initializations,
which break the encapsulation. I do not like that.

> Also, should that return from the conditional on init_static_hmc
> failing be 0 or something indicating a failure to initialize?

I'd rather it fail with 0, because it means that command.hpp is not
configured correctly. Remember all of these things get called
in unit-tests so they'd pop up in tests before we make them visible
to users.
> I'd be happy to go through and do the refactoring.

Just be aware that you'll have to hit other code that uses the
sampler pointers -- or at least you'll have to convert to pointers
at some place. I don't think (pointer == 0) is used anywhere
so that shouldn't be a problem, but just in case.

> P.S. I'd also much rather see the numerically obfuscated switch replaced
> with an if-then structure. But I can see how reasonable people would
> differ on this preference.

I draw the line after two nested ifs, especially when they're repeated
this much. An explicit if/then would be a nightmare to read, which is
why I went to a single switch with the built up index.

> P.P.S. Why static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged); Isn't adapt_engaged already
> boolean? You just want to be explicit?

Cast to an int for courtesy before being used in the integer arithmetic
that builds up the unique sampler index.

> P.P.P.S. It's good style to declare variables close to where you define them.
> The sampler_ptr was defined way before the case statement to set it
> and not used in between. But that'll be moot once we get rid of
> the pointers.

That's an artifact of only having HMC samplers at the moment. If we have
another sampler then it would have used the same sampler_ptr.

On 11/14/13, 4:09 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> In fact, I'd be tempted to have the sampler class have a flag indicating
>> whether to call that init_static thing so that it's part of sample, as in:
>>
>> switch (sampler_select) {
>> case 0:
>> return sample(stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc(model,base_rng),
>> ...);
>>
>>
>> template <class S>
>> int sample(S& s, ...) {
>> if (s.requires_init_static())
>> if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(s, algo))
>> return 0;
>> ... do something with s...
>> return 0; // normal return
>> }
>>
>> You could probably just have something like s::requires_init_static
>> as a static boolean class variable so you don't even need a method.
>
> But then we'd have to have each sampler implementation be aware
> of all other implementations through the possible initializations,
> which break the encapsulation. I do not like that.

Agreed. It's a tradeoff, like all coding. You can either repeat
yourself in multiple places or try to make a generalization. But
it's not worth doing if the generalization is forced.

>> Also, should that return from the conditional on init_static_hmc
>> failing be 0 or something indicating a failure to initialize?
>
> I'd rather it fail with 0, because it means that command.hpp is not
> configured correctly.

It that's the case, raise an exception and dump out a message.

The standard thing to do is to trust your code by unit testing,
not put in a run-time test.

> Remember all of these things get called
> in unit-tests so they'd pop up in tests before we make them visible
> to users.
>
>> I'd be happy to go through and do the refactoring.
>
> Just be aware that you'll have to hit other code that uses the
> sampler pointers -- or at least you'll have to convert to pointers
> at some place. I don't think (pointer == 0) is used anywhere
> so that shouldn't be a problem, but just in case.
Of course.

>> P.S. I'd also much rather see the numerically obfuscated switch replaced
>> with an if-then structure. But I can see how reasonable people would
>> differ on this preference.
>
> I draw the line after two nested ifs, especially when they're repeated
> this much. An explicit if/then would be a nightmare to read, which is
> why I went to a single switch with the built up index.

I very strongly disagree.

The way you have it requires lining up how the int gets constructed in
multiple loops via arithmetic and then lining up the resulting magic
numbers with the case statements. The key to readability is having
local decisions made locally.

Luckily, Daniel's going to break this logjam of disagreement with
an even better suggestion --- we write little functions that
do the work for us so the code's both readable, encapsulated, and
has no magic numbers or deeply nested ifs.

I'll call that out in the next e-mail. We'll deal with the refacroring
so you don't have to worry about it.

>> P.P.S. Why static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged); Isn't adapt_engaged already
>> boolean? You just want to be explicit?
>
> Cast to an int for courtesy before being used in the integer arithmetic
> that builds up the unique sampler index.

OK --- I'd rather just rely on how the compiler is specified to
work in these cases, but I'm not adamant about it. Or, use
the logical nature of the boolean in a ternary/conditional operator.

>> P.P.P.S. It's good style to declare variables close to where you define them.
>> The sampler_ptr was defined way before the case statement to set it
>> and not used in between. But that'll be moot once we get rid of
>> the pointers.
>
> That's an artifact of only having HMC samplers at the moment. If we have
> another sampler then it would have used the same sampler_ptr.

Define a new one, then, or refactor the code. Lingering variables
with multiple purposes is just hard to follow (a bad code "smell" as
the refactoring folks would have it).

I know it's Java and ten years plus old, but I'd highly recommend
Fowler's book "Refactoring". It's all about writing code for readability
and maintainability.

- Bob
